draft.title: The Stolen Generations
card: For much of the 20th century, state and territory governments, and some churches and missions, removed First Nations children from their families. The children are known as the Stolen Generations.
Many children were taken under laws that gave officials power over First Nations people. Families often had little or no say, and many children were placed in institutions or with white families.
Children lost contact with family, Country, language and culture. Many were also harmed or neglected in the places they were sent.
The harm did not end when removals did. Families were broken apart, and the loss of connection to family and culture has affected later generations too.
draft.remember: The Stolen Generations were children removed from their families, and the harm has passed down through generations.

a.q: Which statement best describes the Stolen Generations?
opts: First Nations children taken from their families by officials
First Nations adults who were moved to missions to find work
First Nations parents who chose to send children to boarding school
First Nations people who left their communities for the cities
a.why: The Stolen Generations were children taken from their families by governments and churches, often with little or no say for their families. Moving to missions or cities describes other experiences, and the removals were not a choice made by families.
a.clue: Think about who was taken, and who decided.

b.q: Why do historians say the harm of the Stolen Generations continued after the removals ended?
opts: Lost family and cultural ties affected later generations
Removed children were all given lower wages as adults
Governments kept removing children until the present day
Only the children who were removed were ever affected
b.why: Removal cut children off from family, Country, language and culture, and that loss has affected their children and grandchildren. It is not true that only the removed children were affected, because the harm passed across generations.
b.clue: Think about what children and their families lost, and who else that loss touched.
